gloss: To hold something out or put it forward for someone to accept or refuse.
examples: Can I *offer* you something to drink?
They *offered* her the job on Friday.
The store is *offering* free delivery this week.
contrast: Stress falls on the first syllable, so the *r* is not doubled: *offered*, *offering* — never *offerred*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*provide lunch*), intransitive (*provide for a family*)
gloss: To give someone what they need or ask for.
examples: The school *provides* free lunch to every student.
They *provided* blankets after the storm.
We are *providing* transportation for the out-of-town guests.
contrast: Two patterns, both with a preposition: *provide* someone **with** something, or *provide* something **for** someone. Never *provide me a pen*.

gloss: To give or sell someone goods or materials they need, usually regularly.
examples: Two local farms *supply* the restaurant with vegetables.
The company *supplied* the uniforms free of charge.
Who has been *supplying* these parts since the factory closed?
contrast: The *-y* changes: *supplies*, *supplied* — but it stays in *supplying*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*deliver a package*), intransitive (*they deliver on weekends*)
gloss: To take goods, mail, or a message to the place or person they are meant for.
examples: That pharmacy *delivers* until ten at night.
The mail carrier *delivered* the package to the wrong house.
Our order is being *delivered* tomorrow morning.

gloss: To give money, goods, or blood to a charity or other organization.
examples: Many families *donate* clothes in December.
He *donated* his old laptop to the library.
They have been *donating* blood twice a year since college.

transitivity: both — transitive (*contribute an article*), intransitive (*everyone contributed*)
gloss: To give money, effort, or ideas as your part of something shared.
examples: Everyone at work *contributes* five dollars a month.
She *contributed* two hundred dollars to the relief fund.
He has *contributed* three articles to the magazine this year.
contrast: Stress is on the second syllable — kuhn-TRIB-yoot, not CON-tri-byoot — and the money goes **to** something: *contribute to a fund*.

gloss: To give something formally, especially at a ceremony.
examples: They *present* the award every spring.
The mayor *presented* her with a medal for bravery.
She is *presenting* the check to the school on Thursday.
contrast: The verb is pri-ZENT /prɪˈzɛnt/; the noun *a present* (a gift) is PREZ-uhnt /ˈprɛznt/.

gloss: To pass something to someone using your hands.
examples: Please *hand* me the scissors.
He *handed* the keys to his brother without a word.
The waiter is *handing* each guest a menu.

transitivity: both — transitive (*share a room*), intransitive (*children learn to share*)
gloss: To have or use something together with someone else, or to give part of it away.
examples: The two boys *share* a bedroom.
She *shared* her notes with the whole class.
They have been *sharing* a car since March.
contrast: You *share* something **with** a person: *share the pizza with me*, not *share me the pizza*.

gloss: To hand or spread something out to a number of people or places.
examples: Volunteers *distribute* water at every mile of the race.
The teacher *distributed* the tests face down.
Aid is being *distributed* by helicopter.

gloss: To give out something official, such as a document, a permit, or a statement.
examples: The office *issues* parking permits on Mondays.
The court *issued* a warrant that same afternoon.
They are *issuing* refunds to everyone who paid the old rate.

gloss: To give someone something officially, especially permission or a right.
examples: The city *grants* permits to only ten vendors a year.
The judge *granted* the request without comment.
He was *granted* citizenship last spring.
contrast: American /æ/: GRANT rhymes with *ant*, not with the British /ɑː/.

gloss: To give someone a prize, a sum of money, or a contract as an official decision.
examples: They *award* one full scholarship a year.
The jury *awarded* her two million dollars.
He has been *awarded* three patents since 2019.

gloss: To set aside a share of money, time, or space for a particular purpose.
examples: We *allocate* twenty percent of the budget to travel.
The city *allocated* the funds to three schools.
They are *allocating* seats by lottery this year.

gloss: To give each person or purpose a fixed amount or share.
examples: They *allot* each speaker ten minutes.
The school *allotted* us two parking spaces.
Only an hour was *allotted* for questions.
contrast: Stress on the last syllable doubles the *t*: *allotted*, *allotting*.

gloss: To give out measured amounts of something, especially medicine or supplies.
examples: The machine *dispenses* coffee, tea, and hot chocolate.
The nurse *dispensed* the medication herself.
They are *dispensing* free masks at the entrance.

gloss: To supply someone with what they need, or to put furniture in a room.
examples: The landlord *furnishes* the sheets and towels.
They *furnished* the police with a full description.
Every unit in the building is *furnished*.
contrast: *Furnish* someone **with** something: *furnished us with a map*.

gloss: To supply a person or place with the tools or equipment needed for something.
examples: The district *equips* every classroom with a projector.
They *equipped* the van with a wheelchair ramp.
The crew is *equipping* the shelter for winter.
contrast: Stress on the last syllable doubles the *p*: *equipped*, *equipping*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*submit a form*), intransitive (*he refused to submit*)
gloss: To hand in a document or piece of work for someone to consider.
examples: You *submit* the application online.
She *submitted* her résumé on Tuesday.
He has *submitted* the same essay twice.
contrast: Stress on the last syllable doubles the *t*: *submitted*, *submitting*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*surrender your passport*), intransitive (*the soldiers surrendered*)
gloss: To give something up to someone else, especially because you are forced to.
examples: You must *surrender* your license at the front desk.
The driver *surrendered* his keys without arguing.
They are *surrendering* the property to the bank next month.

transitivity: both — transitive (*sacrifice a weekend*), intransitive (*parents sacrifice*)
gloss: To give up something you value in order to get or protect something else.
examples: Parents often *sacrifice* their own plans for their kids.
She *sacrificed* a whole weekend to finish the project.
He has *sacrificed* a lot for that career.
contrast: The ending is /faɪs/ with an *s* sound — SAK-ruh-fyss, not "-fyze".

gloss: To give your time, money, or effort entirely to one thing.
examples: They *devote* every Sunday to family.
He *devoted* thirty years to that school.
She is *devoting* her savings to the trip.
contrast: *Devote* something **to** something: *devoted his life to teaching*.

gloss: To set something aside for one purpose, or to name a work in someone's honor.
examples: They *dedicate* one small room to storage.
The author *dedicated* the book to her mother.
A bench has been *dedicated* to him in the park.

gloss: To give something or someone into another person's care, trusting them with it.
examples: I would *entrust* him with anything.
She *entrusted* the money to her sister.
The files were *entrusted* to a lawyer downtown.
contrast: Two patterns: *entrust* someone **with** something, or *entrust* something **to** someone.

transitivity: both — transitive (*confer a degree*), intransitive (*confer with a colleague*)
gloss: To grant someone an honor, a title, or a right formally.
examples: The university *confers* degrees in May.
The title was *conferred* on him in 1998.
The judges are *conferring* before they announce a winner.
contrast: Stress on the last syllable doubles the *r*: *conferred*, *conferring*.

gloss: To give something to someone as a present, with no payment expected.
examples: Her parents *gift* the kids books every birthday.
A neighbor *gifted* us a set of kitchen chairs.
The land was *gifted* to the town in 1970.

transitivity: both — transitive (*serve dinner*), intransitive (*they serve until nine*)
gloss: To bring food or drink to someone, or to attend to customers.
examples: That diner *serves* breakfast all day.
He *served* the soup before the salad.
We are *serving* about two hundred people tonight.

gloss: To pay for something enjoyable for someone else as a gift.
examples: Let me *treat* you to lunch.
Her uncle *treated* everyone to ice cream.
He is *treating* the whole team to dinner tonight.
contrast: *Treat* someone **to** something: *treated us to coffee*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*tip the driver*), intransitive (*Americans tip well*)
gloss: To give a server, driver, or other worker extra money for their service.
examples: Americans usually *tip* about twenty percent.
We *tipped* the driver ten dollars.
She is *tipping* in cash tonight.
contrast: Short vowel plus one consonant doubles it: *tipped*, *tipping*.

gloss: To give someone something in return for good work or good behavior.
examples: Good schools *reward* effort, not just talent.
The company *rewarded* her with a bonus.
Honest work is rarely *rewarded* that quickly.

transitivity: both — transitive (*compensate the workers*), intransitive (*compensate for a loss*)
gloss: To pay someone money to make up for a loss, injury, or inconvenience.
examples: The airline will *compensate* passengers for the delay.
They *compensated* him for the damage to his fence.
Nothing is *compensating* us for the lost weekend.

gloss: To pay someone back money they have already spent.
examples: The company *reimburses* travel costs within reason.
They *reimbursed* me two weeks after I sent the receipts.
Her tuition is being *reimbursed* by her employer.

gloss: To give a customer back the money they paid.
examples: They *refund* the deposit at checkout.
The store *refunded* the full price without asking questions.
My ticket has not been *refunded* yet.
contrast: The verb is ri-FUND /rɪˈfʌnd/; the noun *a refund* is REE-fund /ˈriːfʌnd/.

transitivity: both — transitive (*transfer the money*), intransitive (*she transferred to another school*)
gloss: To move money, property, or a person from one place or owner to another.
examples: You can *transfer* the money online in a minute.
She *transferred* two thousand dollars to his account.
They are *transferring* him to a hospital in Denver.
contrast: Stress on the last syllable doubles the *r*: *transferred*, *transferring*. The noun *a transfer* shifts the stress: TRANS-fur.

gloss: To pass something on to someone, especially a message, a feeling, or property.
examples: Please *convey* my thanks to your parents.
The letter *conveyed* the news as gently as possible.
Nothing in his voice was *conveying* anger.
contrast: A vowel before the *y* keeps it: *conveys*, *conveyed* — not *convies*, *convied*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*pass the salt*), intransitive (*the car passed on the left*)
gloss: To hand or move something from one person to the next.
examples: Could you *pass* the salt?
He *passed* me a note under the table.
The usher is *passing* each guest a program.
contrast: The past tense is *passed* with *-ed*; *past* is a different word — *we walked past the store*.

gloss: To go somewhere, pick something up, and bring it back.
examples: Would you *fetch* a chair from the kitchen?
The dog *fetched* the stick every single time.
She is *fetching* water from the pump out back.

gloss: To give one thing and receive another in its place.
examples: You can *exchange* it for a larger size.
They *exchanged* phone numbers at the party.
We have been *exchanging* letters for almost ten years.
contrast: *Exchange* one thing **for** another: *exchanged the shirt for a jacket*.

gloss: To trade one thing for another, usually informally.
examples: Let's *swap* seats — I can't see the board.
They *swapped* shifts without telling the manager.
The kids are *swapping* stickers again.
contrast: Short vowel plus one consonant doubles it: *swapped*, *swapping*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*trade cards*), intransitive (*the store trades in antiques*)
gloss: To give something to someone and get something of theirs in return.
examples: I'll *trade* you my sandwich for your apple.
He *traded* his bike for an old guitar.
They are *trading* baseball cards at recess.

transitivity: both — transitive (*return the book*), intransitive (*she returned Monday*)
gloss: To give something back to the person or place it came from.
examples: You can *return* it within thirty days.
He *returned* the library books a week late.
The money is being *returned* to the donors.

gloss: To put money into a bank account, or to place something somewhere for safekeeping.
examples: I *deposit* my paycheck every other Friday.
She *deposited* the check from her phone.
The refund has already been *deposited*.
contrast: Stress is on the middle syllable, so nothing doubles: *deposited*, *depositing*.

gloss: To send on a letter, message, or email to someone else.
examples: Please *forward* the email to my manager.
He *forwarded* the message to the whole team by mistake.
Her mail is being *forwarded* to the new address.

transitivity: both — transitive (*ship an order*), intransitive (*it ships Monday*)
gloss: To send goods to a customer or another place, by any kind of transport.
examples: We *ship* anywhere in the country.
They *shipped* the order the same day I paid.
Your package is *shipping* tonight.
contrast: Short vowel plus one consonant doubles it: *shipped*, *shipping*.

gloss: To send a letter or package through the postal service.
examples: I'll *mail* the forms tomorrow.
She *mailed* the check on Friday afternoon.
They are *mailing* the tickets to your home address.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *male*. Americans *mail* a letter where British speakers *post* it.

transitivity: both — transitive (*post a photo*), intransitive (*he posts every day*)
gloss: To put a notice, message, or picture where others can see it, especially online.
examples: They *post* the schedule every Sunday night.
She *posted* the photos about an hour ago.
He has been *posting* about the sale all week.

transitivity: both — transitive (*divide the cake*), intransitive (*the road divides here*)
gloss: To separate something into parts and give each part to someone.
examples: We always *divide* the check evenly.
She *divided* the cake into eight pieces.
The money is being *divided* among the four cousins.
contrast: *Divide* something **between** two people, **among** three or more.

gloss: To give out something scarce in small fixed amounts.
examples: We *ration* the water on long hikes.
The government *rationed* sugar during the war.
They are *rationing* the last of the fuel.
contrast: The *n* never doubles: *rationed*, *rationing*.

gloss: To give someone a task, a place, or a share as their responsibility.
examples: They *assign* one mentor to each new hire.
The teacher *assigned* three chapters over the break.
I have been *assigned* to the night shift.
contrast: The *g* is silent: uh-SYN, one syllable at the end, not "uh-SIG-n".

transitivity: both — transitive (*pledge a donation*), intransitive (*call in and pledge*)
gloss: To promise formally to give money or support.
examples: Listeners *pledge* money during the fundraiser every spring.
The company *pledged* a million dollars to the rebuild.
They have *pledged* to match every donation.

transitivity: both — transitive (*promise a raise*), intransitive (*I promise*)
gloss: To tell someone firmly that you will give them something or do something.
examples: I *promise* to bring it back tomorrow.
He *promised* her a ride home.
She has *promised* the same thing twice already.
contrast: Written *-ise* but pronounced *-iss* /ɪs/, never like *-ize*.

gloss: To promise that something will happen or that a product will work.
examples: We *guarantee* delivery in two business days.
The shop *guaranteed* the repair for a full year.
Nothing is *guaranteed* in this business.
contrast: Silent *u* after the *g*, and the *-ee* just takes a *d*: *guaranteed*, but *guaranteeing* keeps all three *e*s.

transitivity: both — transitive (*volunteer your time*), intransitive (*she volunteers at the shelter*)
gloss: To offer your time or help freely, without being asked or paid.
examples: Several parents *volunteer* at the book fair.
He *volunteered* to drive everyone home.
She has been *volunteering* at the animal shelter since June.

transitivity: both — transitive (*propose a plan*), intransitive (*he proposed to her*)
gloss: To put forward an idea or plan for others to consider.
examples: They *propose* a new schedule every single year.
She *proposed* a much simpler solution.
A tax increase is being *proposed* again.

transitivity: both — transitive (*extend an offer*), intransitive (*the road extends north*)
gloss: To offer something such as credit, an invitation, or thanks to someone.
examples: The bank *extends* credit to small businesses.
They *extended* an invitation to the whole family.
The deadline is being *extended* by a week.

gloss: To add money to someone's account.
examples: They *credit* the refund to your card automatically.
The store *credited* my account the next day.
Twenty dollars has been *credited* to your balance.
contrast: Stress is on the first syllable, so the *t* never doubles: *credited*, *crediting*.

gloss: To provide the money that something needs in order to happen.
examples: Donations *fund* most of the program.
The city *funded* the repairs last year.
The research is being *funded* by a private foundation.

gloss: To supply the money for something large, often as a loan.
examples: Banks *finance* most projects of this size.
They *financed* the car over five years.
The building is being *financed* by the state.

gloss: To pay for an event, a team, or a person, usually in return for publicity.
examples: Local businesses *sponsor* the team every season.
A bank *sponsored* the concert last summer.
They are *sponsoring* three students this year.

gloss: To let someone have or do something.
examples: They *allow* dogs on the patio.
The teacher *allowed* us an extra day.
Photography is not *allowed* inside the museum.
contrast: *Allowed* sounds exactly like *aloud*: *they allowed him to speak*, but *read it aloud*.

gloss: To officially allow someone to have or do something.
examples: The rules *permit* one guest per resident.
They *permitted* him to stay one more night.
Parking is not *permitted* after six.
contrast: Stress on the last syllable doubles the *t*: *permitted*, *permitting*. The noun *a permit* shifts the stress: PUR-mit.

gloss: To let something or someone go, or to make something available to the public.
examples: They *release* the results on Friday.
The hospital *released* him after two days.
The album is being *released* in March.
contrast: Written *-ase* but pronounced *-eess* /iːs/, not *-eez*.

gloss: To choose not to demand a fee, a rule, or a right you are entitled to.
examples: They will *waive* the application fee for students.
The bank *waived* the charge after I called.
Late fees are being *waived* this month.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *wave*, but the spellings split: you *waive a fee* and *wave your hand*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*yield a profit*), intransitive (*yield to oncoming traffic*)
gloss: To produce or give something, or to give way to someone else.
examples: These trees *yield* about forty pounds of fruit a season.
The search *yielded* nothing useful.
The old rules are *yielding* to new ones.
contrast: *i* before *e*: y-i-e-l-d.

gloss: To lose or give up something as a penalty for breaking a rule or agreement.
examples: You *forfeit* the deposit if you cancel late.
They *forfeited* the game when only four players showed up.
He has *forfeited* his right to appeal.
contrast: The *ei* is only /ɪ/: FAWR-fit, not "for-FEET".

gloss: To get something that is sent or given to you.
examples: We *receive* about fifty applications a week.
She *received* the package yesterday.
He has *received* no answer at all.
contrast: *i* before *e* except after *c*: rec**ei**ve, not *recieve*.

gloss: To take something that is offered, or to agree to it.
examples: That truck *accepts* cash only.
She *accepted* the job offer on the spot.
His apology was *accepted* quietly.
contrast: Not the same word as *except*: *accept* means take, *except* means leave out — *everyone except me accepted*.

gloss: To get something, especially by effort or through an official process.
examples: You *obtain* the form at the front desk.
They *obtained* a copy of the contract.
The permit was *obtained* in a single afternoon.

gloss: To come to own or gain something, often gradually or by buying it.
examples: Museums rarely *acquire* work this expensive.
The company *acquired* two smaller firms last year.
She has *acquired* a taste for very strong coffee.
contrast: Spelled with *cq*: a**cq**uire, never *aquire*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*gain access*), intransitive (*the stock gained today*)
gloss: To get something useful, or to increase in amount.
examples: Members *gain* access to the entire library.
He *gained* fifteen pounds over the winter.
She is *gaining* confidence every week.

gloss: To reach or achieve something you have worked toward.
examples: Few runners ever *attain* that kind of speed.
She *attained* the rank of captain at thirty.
The goal has not been *attained* yet.

transitivity: both — transitive (*collect the fares*), intransitive (*water collects in the basement*)
gloss: To gather things together, or to obtain money that is owed.
examples: He *collects* old road maps.
The driver *collected* the fares at the door.
They are *collecting* donations in the lobby.

transitivity: both — transitive (*gather the papers*), intransitive (*a crowd gathered*)
gloss: To bring things or people together into one place.
examples: Squirrels *gather* nuts all through the fall.
A crowd *gathered* outside the courthouse.
We are *gathering* signatures for the petition.

gloss: To collect a very large amount of something over time.
examples: Few people *amass* that kind of wealth honestly.
He *amassed* a collection of ten thousand records.
They have *amassed* enough evidence to file charges.

gloss: To gather up more and more of something over a period of time.
examples: Dust *accumulates* fast in this room.
She *accumulated* six weeks of unused vacation.
Snow has been *accumulating* since midnight.
contrast: Double *c*, single *m*: a**cc**umulate.

gloss: To collect and hide away a large supply of something, often more than you need.
examples: Some shoppers *hoard* bottled water before a storm.
He *hoarded* newspapers for forty years.
People were *hoarding* canned food that spring.
contrast: Sounds like *horde* (*a horde of tourists*), but *hoard* is the verb for storing things away.

gloss: To receive money for work, or to deserve something by what you do.
examples: Servers here *earn* most of their money in tips.
She *earned* every dollar of that raise.
He has *earned* a reputation for being fair.
contrast: The *ea* is /ɜːr/, as in *learn* — the word sounds exactly like *urn*.

gloss: To ask for and take something that belongs to you by right.
examples: You *claim* your bags at carousel four.
Nobody ever *claimed* the wallet.
She is *claiming* the money her aunt left her.

gloss: To ask for something politely or formally.
examples: Guests may *request* a late checkout.
He *requested* a copy of the report.
A second opinion has been *requested*.
contrast: No *for* after this verb: *request a copy*, not "request for a copy" — the *for* belongs to *ask for*.

gloss: To ask for something forcefully, as if you have a right to it.
examples: Customers *demand* a refund when it breaks this fast.
She *demanded* an explanation.
They are *demanding* a full investigation.
contrast: American /æ/ — di-MAND rhymes with *hand*. And no *for*: *demand an answer*.

gloss: To need something, or to make something a condition.
examples: The job *requires* two years of experience.
They *required* a deposit up front.
A signature is *required* on both copies.

transitivity: both — transitive (*beg a favor*), intransitive (*begging on the corner*)
gloss: To ask for something urgently, or to ask strangers for money.
examples: The kids *beg* for dessert every single night.
He *begged* her to stay.
A man was *begging* outside the station.
contrast: Short vowel plus one consonant doubles it: *begged*, *begging*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*order a pizza*), intransitive (*are you ready to order?*)
gloss: To ask a restaurant or a store to supply something.
examples: We usually *order* the same thing.
She *ordered* two pizzas for the whole group.
He has *ordered* three books this month.

gloss: To arrange for something to be kept for you to use later.
examples: They *reserve* the front row for family.
I *reserved* a table for seven o'clock.
That whole section is *reserved*.

gloss: To receive money, property, or traits from someone who has died or come before you.
examples: The children *inherit* everything equally.
She *inherited* the farm from her grandfather.
He has *inherited* his father's temper.
contrast: Stress is in the middle, so nothing doubles: *inherited*, *inheriting*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*harvest the corn*), intransitive (*they harvest in October*)
gloss: To gather a crop when it is ripe.
examples: They *harvest* the corn in late September.
We *harvested* four bushels of apples in one afternoon.
The wheat is being *harvested* right now.

gloss: To receive the results of something you did earlier, good or bad.
examples: Investors *reap* the profits, not the workers.
She *reaped* the benefits of all those early mornings.
They are still *reaping* rewards from that one decision.

gloss: To take something quickly and by force, or to take it by legal authority.
examples: Customs officers sometimes *seize* packages like this.
Police *seized* the car as evidence.
The property is being *seized* by the bank.
contrast: An exception to "i before e": s**ei**ze, not *sieze*.

gloss: To catch and hold a person, an animal, or a moment.
examples: These traps *capture* the mice alive.
The photo *captured* the whole street at sunrise.
Two of them were *captured* near the border.

gloss: To take hold of something quickly and roughly.
examples: *Grab* a coat — it's colder than it looks.
He *grabbed* my arm before I slipped.
She is *grabbing* coffee on the way in.
contrast: Short vowel plus one consonant doubles it: *grabbed*, *grabbing*.

gloss: To take something suddenly and rudely out of someone's hands.
examples: Gulls will *snatch* food right out of your hand.
Someone *snatched* her purse on the platform.
The dog is *snatching* bread off the counter again.

gloss: To take someone's property away officially, as a punishment or for safety.
examples: Teachers here *confiscate* phones during tests.
The guard *confiscated* his lighter at the gate.
Anything sharp is *confiscated* at security.

gloss: To get something back from the place where it was left or stored.
examples: The app *retrieves* your old messages.
He *retrieved* the ball from the neighbor's roof.
She is *retrieving* her coat from the closet.
contrast: *ie*, not *ei* — retr**ie**ve, even though *receive* goes the other way.

transitivity: both — transitive (*recover the bikes*), intransitive (*he recovered slowly*)
gloss: To get back something that was lost, stolen, or spent.
examples: Divers sometimes *recover* things from the bottom of the lake.
Police *recovered* the stolen bikes two blocks away.
Two of the paintings have been *recovered*.

gloss: To get back something that was taken from you or given up.
examples: You can *reclaim* the tax at the airport.
She *reclaimed* the land after a ten-year fight.
The city is *reclaiming* the old rail yard.

gloss: To save what can still be used from something damaged or destroyed.
examples: Crews still *salvage* metal from that wreck.
We *salvaged* what we could after the flood.
They are *salvaging* bricks from the old school.

gloss: To take a child or an animal into your family permanently, or to take up an idea as your own.
examples: Many families *adopt* through this agency.
They *adopted* a dog from the county shelter.
She was *adopted* as a baby.
contrast: Not *adapt*: you *adopt* a child, but you *adapt* to the cold. Nothing doubles: *adopted*, *adopting*.

gloss: To greet someone kindly when they arrive, or to accept something gladly.
examples: Good hotels *welcome* returning guests by name.
They *welcomed* us with coffee and warm bread.
New members are always *welcomed* warmly.
contrast: One *l*: *welcome*, not *wellcome*. The final *e* drops only before *-ing*: *welcoming*.

gloss: To say hello to someone when you meet them.
examples: The owner *greets* everyone at the door.
She *greeted* him with a hug.
We were *greeted* by a wall of noise.

gloss: To hug someone, or to accept an idea eagerly.
examples: Younger shoppers *embrace* the new payment app.
He *embraced* his brother at the gate.
The idea has been *embraced* by both parties.

gloss: To put money in your pocket, especially money you should not keep.
examples: Middlemen *pocket* most of the difference.
He *pocketed* the change without counting it.
She is *pocketing* half the profit.
contrast: Stress is on the first syllable, so the *t* never doubles: *pocketed*, *pocketing*.

gloss: To succeed in getting something valuable, often with effort.
examples: Good agents *secure* better deals.
They *secured* funding for another year.
A second interview has been *secured*.

gloss: To buy something — the more formal word for *buy*.
examples: Members *purchase* tickets at a discount.
She *purchased* the house in cash.
The equipment was *purchased* two years ago.
contrast: The *-ase* is unstressed /əs/: PUR-chuhss, never "pur-CHAYSS".

gloss: To take something for a while and give it back later.
examples: Students can *borrow* six books at a time.
I *borrowed* his car for the weekend.
She has been *borrowing* money from her sister for months.
contrast: You *borrow* **from** someone; they *lend* **to** you. Russian *одолжить* covers both directions, English does not.

transitivity: both — transitive (*rent a truck*), intransitive (*the place rents for $900*)
gloss: To pay to use something for a period of time, or to let someone use it for payment.
examples: We *rent* a place near the water every July.
He *rented* a truck for the move.
The apartment has already been *rented*.
contrast: *Rent* works in both directions: you *rent from* a landlord, and a landlord *rents to* you.

ru: арендовать, сдавать в аренду, взять в аренду
gloss: To rent property or equipment under a long written contract.
examples: Most drivers here *lease* their cars.
The company *leased* two floors downtown.
The land is being *leased* to a solar farm.
contrast: Ends in /s/, not /z/ — LEESS, rhyming with *piece*.

gloss: To let someone use your money or property for a while.
examples: Neighbors *loan* each other tools all the time.
He *loaned* me two hundred dollars until payday.
The painting is *loaned* to the museum every fall.
contrast: Americans use *loan* as a verb where the British prefer *lend*. It sounds like *lone*.

gloss: To give someone a job or pay them for a service.
examples: They *hire* extra staff every December.
She *hired* a lawyer the same afternoon.
The restaurant is *hiring* again.
contrast: In American English *hire* means to employ a person; for a car or a tool Americans say *rent*, not *hire*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*charge a fee*), intransitive (*they charge by the hour*)
gloss: To ask someone for a particular amount of money for goods or a service.
examples: They *charge* five dollars for parking.
The plumber *charged* us double on a Sunday.
You are being *charged* a monthly fee.
contrast: *Charge* someone **for** something, and *charge* it **to** a card.

gloss: To send someone a written request for payment.
examples: They *bill* the insurance company directly.
The clinic *billed* me twice for one visit.
You will be *billed* at the end of the month.

gloss: To have to pay someone money you have not paid yet.
examples: I *owe* my sister forty dollars.
He *owed* the bank more than he made in a year.
They still have not paid what is *owed*.
contrast: The *w* is silent — *owe* is just /oʊ/, like *oh*. Add *-d* for *owed*, but drop the *e* for *owing*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*decline an offer*), intransitive (*sales declined*)
gloss: To politely refuse something that is offered.
examples: They politely *decline* most invitations.
She *declined* the offer twice.
My card was *declined* at the register.

transitivity: both — transitive (*refuse the money*), intransitive (*he simply refused*)
gloss: To say firmly that you will not take or do something.
examples: Some drivers *refuse* to take cash.
He *refused* the money outright.
She is *refusing* to sign anything.
contrast: The verb is ri-FYOOZ /rɪˈfjuːz/; the noun *refuse* (trash) is REF-yooss /ˈrɛfjuːs/.

gloss: To refuse to accept a person, an offer, or an application.
examples: Editors *reject* most of what they get.
The bank *rejected* his application.
Her proposal was *rejected* without a vote.
contrast: The verb is ri-JEKT /rɪˈdʒɛkt/; the noun *a reject* is REE-jekt /ˈriːdʒɛkt/.

gloss: To refuse to give someone something they ask for.
examples: They *deny* him access to the files.
His visa was *denied* twice.
The board is *denying* every request this quarter.
contrast: Consonant plus *-y*: *denies*, *denied* — but the *y* stays in *denying*.

gloss: To take away from someone something they need or are entitled to.
examples: Long shifts *deprive* nurses of sleep.
The new rule *deprived* him of a hearing.
They were *deprived* of clean water for a week.
contrast: *Deprive* someone **of** something — the *of* is not optional.

gloss: To take money or property from a person or place by force or threat.
examples: They *rob* the same stretch of highway every winter.
Two men *robbed* the store right at closing.
He has been *robbed* twice this year.
contrast: Short vowel plus one consonant doubles it: *robbed*, *robbing*. You *rob* a person or a bank, but you *steal* a thing.

gloss: To take an amount away from a total, especially from a payment.
examples: They *deduct* taxes from every paycheck.
The hotel *deducted* the deposit from the bill.
Union dues are *deducted* automatically.

transitivity: both — transitive (*save money*), intransitive (*they save for retirement*)
gloss: To keep money or things instead of spending or using them.
examples: We *save* about three hundred dollars a month.
She *saved* for two years to buy it.
They have been *saving* every coupon in a drawer.

gloss: To ask someone to come to an event or to join you.
examples: They *invite* the whole block every Fourth of July.
She *invited* us to stay the night.
He has not been *invited* yet.
contrast: The verb is in-VYT; the informal noun *an invite* shifts the stress to IN-vyt.
